study.name: When mere action versus inaction leads to robust preference change
study.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
study.citation: Chen, Z., Holland, R. W., Quandt, J., Dijksterhuis, A., & Veling, H. (2019). When mere action versus inaction leads to robust preference change. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 117(4), 721-740. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspa0000158
study.description: Preregistered, seven experiments; materials and data at https://osf.io/zy9w3/.

description: Willingness-to-pay for 60 packaged snacks, elicited in a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak auction. Participants were given 2 euros and bid EUR 0-2 for each snack by moving a cursor along an analog scale, knowing one snack would be drawn and played for real; they had fasted for at least three hours. Every snack was bid on twice, once before and once after go/no-go training, which is what timepoints 1 and 2 hold -- the study's question is whether merely responding to an item shifts what it is worth. Stimuli are Dutch supermarket snacks and the source files identify them only by image number, so item names were read off the packaging in the stimulus photographs published with the experiment programs; the resolved key ships beside this ingest. International brands use the spelling already in the database so they join existing items; Dutch products keep their Dutch product name. Choices during training were made under a 1.5 s deadline. Eight training repetitions.
